blocks.text: The intermolecular forces among the molecules of a liquid are reasonably strong. Three types are described here: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces), permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding.

blocks.alt: Left: two electron clouds with a momentary plus and minus end attracting each other, boiling point lists for the halogens, noble gases and alkanes, and stick drawings of the three pentane isomers. Middle: three HCl molecules lined up plus to minus, and three water molecules joined by dotted hydrogen bonds. Right: notes on ammonia and hydrogen fluoride, an HF zig-zag chain, and a box counting hydrogen bonds per molecule.
blocks.caption: London forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding (original diagram after Figures 5.2 to 5.5 and Tables 5.1 and 5.2).
blocks.long_description: A momentary unevenness of one electron cloud induces a dipole in a neighbour, giving the London force that acts between all molecules and is the only force in non-polar substances; it grows with molecular mass and with surface area, so boiling points rise from F2 to I2, from He to Xe, from methane to decane, and from compact neopentane to straight n-pentane. Polar molecules such as HCl and chloroform also line up plus end to minus end. When hydrogen is bonded to F, O or N that has a lone pair, the strongest intermolecular force, the hydrogen bond, forms: two per water molecule, one per ammonia (one lone pair) and one per HF (one hydrogen).
